en: An Excerpt from the Commentary on the *Mahāyānacaturdharmaka-sūtra* Regarding the establishment of the titles of sūtras, they are all formulated based on four criteria:
first, by way of the person [who spoke it], such as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and others; second, by way of the location [where it was spoken], such as the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.
In the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*,
the World-Honored One addressed the King of Laṅkā, named Rāvaṇa,
and preached the Dharma on Mount Laṅkā.
Thus, he established their names by means of a convention.
As for the "three dharmas," they are as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*: the dharmas of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and so forth.
Both internal and external are empty, for one does not cling to the two selves of person and phenomena;
thus, this name is established in terms of dharmas. As for the four similes:
As stated in the *Ratnamegha Sūtra* and other texts, when that sūtra was being preached,
bodhisattvas from the ten directions all gathered like clouds.
Establishing the Name by Way of Analogy. Question:
By what means is this sūtra named in relation to these four categories? Answer:
This present sūtra is named in relation to the Dharma.
What is that method?
It consists in not abandoning the bodhicitta and not abandoning solitude and the like.
It is so. Regarding the phrase "the object of focus" and "the greatness of practice":
it refers to the extensive cultivation of both one's own practice and the practice for others.
Regarding "practicing for oneself," this refers to the cultivation of the six perfections and so forth.
Among these six perfections,
the first three constitute practice for others.
The latter two are practices for one's own benefit.
As for diligence, it is the practice of benefiting others;
if there are sentient beings...
Those who are to be liberated by means of a Buddha-body,
for them he manifests a Buddha-body, as well as the bodies of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas,
and so forth. This is because these four dharmas, when combined, are capable of giving rise to the bodhicitta and encompassing the practices of both self-benefit and benefiting others.
Furthermore, it is explained that not abandoning the bodhicitta is the practice for oneself,
while skillfully knowing how to dwell happily in secluded places and so forth is the practice for the benefit of others;
likewise, mental humility and gentleness are the practices for the benefit of others.
Regarding the greatness of wisdom:
it realizes that both persons and phenomena are empty;
this differs from the śrāvakas, who are only able to realize the emptiness of persons.
Not for the sake of the emptiness of phenomena; therefore, they abide in nirvāṇa,
benefiting others without a body.
Unlike ordinary beings, who all fail to realize they are bound by afflictions,
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
because they have realized the emptiness of persons, do not abide in saṃsāra.
Because they have realized the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), they do not abide in nirvāṇa.
Regarding the greatness of their diligence:
during the first incalculable eon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), they bring the four preparatory practices (*prayoga*) to perfection; during the second incalculable eon...
From the first stage to the eighth stage,

one cultivates and achieves the path of vision (darśanamārga) over three incalculable eons (asaṃkhyeyakalpa). From the eighth stage to the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), [one cultivates the path of meditation].
For example, when Śāriputra was practicing the bodhisattva path, there was a brahmin who begged for his eyes;
he then gave them to him. Upon receiving the eyes, the brahmin rubbed them with his foot.
Śāriputra then asked, "For what reason do you polish it?
He replied:
I desire its sound;
it is said that its skillful means are great,
as explained above regarding the greatness of wisdom.
Regarding what is called "great karma":
it is that which, throughout the entire cycle of birth and death, enables one to become a Buddha;
as for the "vehicle," it is that which enables one to give rise to the four vows.
The vow is great:
if there should be even a single sentient being who does not attain Buddhahood,
I vow not to seek unexcelled bodhi.
Unlike the śrāvakas, who do not give rise to great vows and thus cannot achieve the ten powers,
those who accomplish the great [vows] are able to achieve the ten powers.
Because of its great merit, such as the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), and so forth.
Each point is explained as elsewhere.
Regarding the seven great meanings mentioned above,
the first six serve as causes.
Since each individual [element] cannot by itself accomplish the ten powers and so forth,
it is necessary to cultivate these six great elements;
the last one serves as the fruit.
As for what are called the four dharma-boats,
they are: not abandoning the bodhicitta and delighting in dwelling in secluded places.
Regarding the enumeration, it is clarified within the treatise itself.
As for the term "giving birth," it means that through the practice of these four dharmas, one is able to emerge from the ocean of death.
Regarding "manifesting through names and titles":
it is able to manifest the profoundly deep nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Regarding "unchanging throughout antiquity and the present": [it remains so].
This accords with the constant meaning [of the Dharma].
From the Buddhas of the past to the Buddhas of the future, there has never been any shifting or addition,
just as it is with the twelve links of dependent origination.
The two characters "fǎjìng" (path of the Dharma) are also to be combined as above.
As for what is called "indicating the location," it refers to the passage from "Thus have I heard" up to "bodhisattva mahāsattva."
Regarding the term "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa), it refers to the three characteristics,
namely the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and so forth.
What is called "phenomena" (dharma) refers to the five aggregates, the eighteen elements, and so forth.
What is called "meaning" (artha) refers to...
This refers to that which expresses the abiding nature of the five aggregates and the eighteen elements.
Regarding the introduction, there are two types: first, initiation through a request; [and second, initiation by the Buddha's own resolve].
Second, it does not arise dependent upon consciousness.
Question:
Why is the introduction concerning the sequence of faith and understanding not explained in detail?
Answer: The introduction establishing faith is common to all sutras and thus does not require further explanation.
Although this has now been briefly clarified,
as for the statement that the Buddha’s conditions for transformation were exhausted, it simply means that those for whom he was to deliver were fully saved.
Because there are none who are not saved due to a lack of conditions.
The Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:
"Although the Buddha's majesty is universal..."
It does not cross over that which is rootless, lacks moisture, or is parched; it does not moisten withered wood.
As for the "four meeting places," this refers to contemplating the impurity of the body.
Because this body is composed of thirty-six kinds of impurities and various other unclean things,
it is called "impure," and so forth. As for the statement that one contemplates feeling as suffering:
Painful feelings, pleasant feelings, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings are all suffering;
yet sentient beings do not understand this.
"I take this to be happiness.
The phrase "Kāśyapa Bodhisattva and others" includes Maitreya and Mañjuśrī.
Regarding the statement that observing the mind is impermanent:
this mind perishes from moment to moment,
yet sentient beings do not realize it.
They grasp at these as having the characteristic of permanence.
As for what is called "contemplating the selflessness of phenomena," it refers to [the contemplation] upon the five aggregates and the eighteen elements.
Originally, there is no such thing as self, person, sentient being, or life-span; yet sentient beings, failing to understand this,
recklessly conceive of a self.
However, by not giving rise to the aforementioned inverted views,
one attains the Noble Path.
"Mouth" refers to the cause.
What is called the "Brahma-maṇḍala" is here translated as "Mopin.
What is called the "Vinaya on Miscellaneous Matters" (Kṣudrakavastu) is...
This is explained within the fifty fascicles of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*.
Regarding the phrase "at the time of the compilation":
it refers to the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
In the Seven-Leaf Rock Cave at Rājagṛha,
he assembled the assembly of five hundred great arhats and requested Ānanda to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma.
The assembly gave rise to three doubts;
these were resolved when Ānanda recited "Thus have I heard" and so forth,
concerning the time when the Buddha first attained enlightenment.
In the Deer Park, he first delivered the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths to the group of five headed by Kaundinya.
Regarding the "three turnings," it is as follows: [and so forth].
Regarding the terms "time," "direction," and "person":
"time" refers to "at one time" within that very sūtra;
"direction" means "place."
"Persons" refers to those who listen to the Dharma.
"Teachings" refers precisely to the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
"Principle" refers to the nature of True Suchness (tathatā).
"Practice" refers to—
This refers to the Eightfold Noble Path.
As for "fruits," this refers to the fruits with superior stages, the unsurpassed fruit, and so forth.
Regarding the statement that obtaining results in accordance with one's vows constitutes "similarity," this refers to such matters as attaining great merit through giving, and so forth.
Regarding the statement that "setting aside the particular to focus on the general," [it means as follows].
There are two meanings:
first, it requires the ear-faculty to give rise to consciousness,
which the mind then follows in its discrimination.
Regarding the statement that "listing each one individually results in prolixity," this is a refutation of an objection which says:
"It would suffice to include only 'root,' 'mind,' and 'consciousness' within the title of the sutra."
"Why do you require me to hear it?
He replied, "The meaning is established as such; were it to be fully elaborated, it would become excessively voluminous. Why, then, not simply cite one [instance]?"
Answer: If one were to cite only a single instance, its meaning would not be fully utilized. Furthermore, an objection is raised:
"If that is so, why is it not found in the sūtras?"
It is said that "I heard" was established in order to lead those of external paths into the Dharma.
Thus, "I heard" was set forth.

Just as the Buddha, through his skillful means, provisionally established the concept of a "self" in response to the questions of the brahmin Dīrghanakha when it was deemed appropriate by the World-Honored One; so too,
when those capable of being transformed were ready for deliverance before the meal, he would deliver them immediately.
If, after eating, one is capable of being saved, then one saves them immediately.
What is called "the resonance of the faculty" is like clear water.
According to the size of the vessel,
the reflection of the moon appears within it,
capable of manifesting reflections that are either large or small.
Regarding the benefit derived from correspondence:
the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas,
[accord with] the root-natures of the three vehicles of sentient beings.
He preaches the Dharma according to the occasion,
causing sentient beings each to obtain benefit,
just like a physician.
By administering the medicine according to whether the illness is cold or hot,
the disease is immediately cured.
It is said that external scriptures lack such efficacy.
There is no teaching established according to the capacity of the recipient,
nor medicine administered according to the illness;
there is not a single word spoken for a specific occasion.
Regarding the exclusion of the listener before the discourse:
in the sūtras of other schools, four factors are excluded.
Regarding the exclusion of the listener after the discourse: [the same applies].
This refers to the meaning of "before eating" and "after eating.
To the objection that "if this were so, all phenomena would not be consciousness-only," the following refutation is offered:
Regarding these four Dharma-discourses,
if we consider them within the three schools of the Mahāyāna,
they are for the time being subsumed under the Vijñaptimātra (Consciousness-Only) school.
Since, as established above, one posits that at a given time there are dharmas external to the mind,
these dharmas should not be mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*).
The answer is identical to the text of the *Viniscaya*.
What is called "cognition of the world" refers to the mundane world, that is, the receptacle-world (*bhājana-loka*).
What is called "cognition of number" refers to...
"One, two, three, four" refers to the Most Victorious Honored One, who is the Buddha.
Regarding "mastery" (vaśitā):
it refers to being unable to be bound by the afflictions of the three realms and nine stages, such as those abandoned through seeing and cultivation,
because one has attained mastery over these afflictions.
Regarding the term "blazing and fierce," it refers to the burning away of the fuel of afflictions by the fire of wisdom.
Regarding the term "exquisite and majestic," [it refers to...]
By revering one's parents, teachers, the Sangha, and preceptors,
one attains the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; thus,
it is called "Auspicious."
Because they are approached, respectfully served, and universally praised, they possess auspiciousness.
It is as in the examples of the blind gaining sight and the mute being able to speak, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "constantly initiating skillful means for the benefit and happiness [of others]":
Worldly benefit and supramundane peace and happiness;
or, it refers to the definitive arising of benefit from superior and excellent peace and happiness.
The term "reversal" (or "covering") signifies the meaning of "noble" (or "honorable").
It is also called diligence (*vīrya*).
Regarding the statement that the Buddha is endowed with ten virtues,
an objection is raised as follows:
Why does it not begin with "The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha," etc.,
but instead simply uses the name "Bhagavān"? Answer:
The phrasing is like a definitive resolution.
To address the objection that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses three bodies, it is said:
From this discussion, further discussion arose;
from this discussion, further speech arose.
Again he asked:
The Buddha has three bodies.
For those of inferior faculties, he teaches by means of the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body);
this transformation body is the sixteen-foot complete body. The *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) is for those on the stages (*bhūmi*).
To those who are to be saved by a Buddha-body,
he manifests a Buddha-body and preaches the Dharma for them.
As for what is called the "retribution body" (sambhogakāya):
It has the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom as its essence;
it takes the differentiated wisdom that conceals the nature of the single True Suchness as its object,
when discussed in terms of the former two bodies.
The Dharma-body appears as if it were speaking; however,
if one discusses it from the perspective of the Dharma-body itself,
there is neither speaking nor non-speaking.
